<reason>A built the cleaner path to victory. Its core route — 25 years of voluntary failure proves an incentive problem, and only a fine reaches the warned, resourced refuser — was never neutralized; B's toolkit (procurement, credits, audits) presupposes cooperation, and B never named a non-fine instrument that touches refusal. The decisive moment came when A's pressure Q2 ("is there any fine design you would accept?") forced B in B4.2 to accept "a genuine last-resort penalty for documented bad-faith refusal," which A's closing fairly captured as the motion itself: the text bars nothing about also funding remediation, and "repeatedly" plus "meaningful" plausibly carry process and proportionality, as A argued directly in A4.1. B's main counter-route depended on (a) a hostile, hyperliteral reading of the motion that A's natural-language reading answers, and (b) the claim that the fined population would be mostly capacity-poor — but B supported that by repurposing A's "most visited pages" statistic, which describes large resourced sites and actually reinforces A's incentives story. B also carried an internal tension: accepting a penalty for documented bad-faith refusal requires exactly the willful-vs-struggling sorting B called impossible. B was genuinely strong — the overlay/compliance-theater and vendor lock-in points were the debate's most original material and its rhetoric matched A's — but after B4.2 it was defending framing rather than substance.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure Q2 cornered B into conceding a last-resort penalty for documented repeat refusal (B4.2); A's closing ("That is the motion") converted it into the winning crystallization, leaving B's closing to re-litigate a framing dispute rather than defend a fine-free alternative.</best_rebuttal>
